meta.title: Who really said "Trying to be happy by accumulating possessions is like trying to satisfy hunger by taping sandwiches all over your body"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not George Carlin. The line is Roger J. Corless's, from The Vision of Buddhism (Paragon House, 1989) — and the original says "my body," not "your body."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Trying to be happy by accumulating possessions is like trying to satisfy hunger by taping sandwiches all over your body'?
meta.ogDescription: Not George Carlin. It's Buddhist scholar Roger J. Corless, in The Vision of Buddhism (1989) — and he wrote "my body," not "your body."

answer.label: Not George Carlin — actually Roger J. Corless
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from The Vision of Buddhism: The Space Under the Tree (New York: Paragon House, 1989) by the Buddhist studies scholar Roger J. Corless — and in the book it reads “all over my body,” not “your body.” The reference site georgecarlin.net lists it among its Bogus Carlin Quotations ↗, noting it appears on none of Carlin’s albums, HBO specials or books — while cautioning that the saying itself may be older than 1989.

source.heading: The actual source

docMeta.dd: The Vision of Buddhism: The Space Under the Tree

source.excerpt: But happiness is not something I have, it is something I myself want to be. Trying to be happy by accumulating possessions is like trying to satisfy hunger by taping sandwiches all over my body.
trail: 1989 — Roger J. Corless publishes The Vision of Buddhism: The Space Under the Tree with Paragon House in New York; the sandwich simile sits in part 2, “The Space.” The edition is held in scan by the Internet Archive ↗ and its bibliographic details are confirmed by a review in the Journal of Asian Studies ↗.
The pronoun swap — WIST ↗ transcribes the original as “all over my body” and records that the line is frequently misattributed to George Carlin in a “your body” form.

The debunk — georgecarlin.net ↗ lists the line among its Bogus Carlin Quotations, names Corless as the apparent real author, notes it appears on no Carlin album, HBO special or book, and adds that the saying may be older than 1989.
Absent from the canon — Wikiquote’s George Carlin page ↗ carries no version of this line in any section, sourced or misattributed.
source.excerptNote: Note the pronoun: Corless wrote my body. The fuller paragraph — which opens by describing how we make ourselves miserable by closing ourselves off from reality and then collecting things in the hope of possessing happiness — is transcribed with its source at WIST ↗. The Internet Archive’s scan of the 1989 edition is borrow-only, so the interior page could not be independently read for this entry; the transcription and its part-level location come from WIST.

source.rightsNote: The Vision of Buddhism: The Space Under the Tree was first published in New York by Paragon House in 1989, so it is firmly within US copyright — the excerpt above is quoted briefly for identification and attribution. The Internet Archive holds the edition on a borrow-only basis, which is consistent with its protected status. No public-domain claim is made for any wording on this page: the “your body” variant that circulates under George Carlin’s name has no identifiable author of its own and no known publication history, and an unsourced meme edit does not create a free text.

author.name: Roger J. Corless
author.heading: Who was Roger J. Corless?
author.metaLine: 1938–2007 · British-born American Buddhist studies scholar · Duke University
author.bio: Roger Corless was born in Merseyside, England in 1938 and spent his career in the United States as Professor of Religion at Duke University, where he specialised in Pure Land Buddhism and Buddhist–Christian dialogue. He co-founded the journal Buddhist-Christian Studies and wrote more than sixty scholarly articles, but his best-known book for general readers is The Vision of Buddhism: The Space Under the Tree (Paragon House, 1989), a survey written in a deliberately plain, wry register. He died in San Francisco in 2007 — almost certainly without knowing that his sandwich simile had begun a second life under a comedian’s name.

misattribution.heading: Two things are wrong with the popular version
misattribution.intro: This is a double error: the wrong name on the byline, and a word swapped in the text. Both are easy to demonstrate.

items.why: The line appears on none of Carlin’s albums, HBO specials or books. georgecarlin.net’s Bogus Carlin Quotations list ↗ puts it under a flat heading saying he did not say it, and observes that it does not even sound like him — he rarely used similes, and his famous routine on possessions, “A Place for My Stuff,” celebrates stuff rather than renouncing it. Wikiquote’s Carlin page ↗ contains no such quotation anywhere.

Corless wrote “taping sandwiches all over my body” — a remark about his own grasping, inside a passage on wanting to be happy rather than to have happiness. The version that travels under Carlin’s name changes it to “your body,” turning self-observation into an accusation. WIST ↗ records the original wording and the swap; georgecarlin.net makes the same point, saying the real author is Corless once you put “my” back.

georgecarlin.net notes that the saying “may be older” than Corless’s book. No earlier printed appearance has been located, so 1989 is the earliest attestation we can point to rather than a proven point of origin. Quote Investigator has not published an investigation of this line.

misattribution.truthLine: The sandwich belongs to a Duke University Buddhist studies professor, not a comedian — and he taped it to his own body. Carlin himself set the test that settles it: per his Wikipedia biography ↗, he stated on his website that nothing online is his unless it came from one of his albums, books, HBO specials, or the site itself. This line comes from none of them.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Carlin
lead: The simile is genuinely good, which is most of the explanation. It is concrete, slightly absurd, and it makes its point in one breath — exactly the shape of a Carlin bit. Once a clever anti-consumerist line is loose on the internet without a source attached, it drifts toward the most famous available anti-consumerist voice, and for a generation of English-speaking readers that voice is George Carlin.

The irony is that the sentiment cuts against his actual material. Carlin’s most celebrated riff on possessions, “A Place for My Stuff” — performed in Carlin on Campus ↗ (1984) — is affectionate about stuff rather than renunciatory about it. georgecarlin.net makes the same observation, adding that he rarely reached for similes at all. The line reads like Carlin to people who remember the target of his jokes but not their texture.
context.detailsSummary: What Carlin said about internet quotes attributed to him
detailsBody: Carlin was aware of the problem in his lifetime. Wikipedia’s article on him records that numerous joke lists, rants and essays circulated falsely under his name, and quotes his own website statement that nothing seen online is his unless it came from one of his albums, books, HBO specials, or his site itself — a test this sandwich line fails on every count. See Wikipedia’s George Carlin article ↗.

Corless’s original sits in a passage about the difference between having happiness and being happy — a Buddhist argument about clinging, not a comic’s bit about consumerism. The switch from “my body” to “your body” quietly changes it from self-observation into finger-pointing, which is also more shareable.
context.pull: A good line with no source attached drifts toward the most famous voice that could plausibly have said it.
